title: How to Run a 30-Minute Weekly Team Meeting That Replaces the Hour You Have Now
author: Nick Martin
summary: Nick Martin argues that the typical weekly team meeting wastes its hour because a round of status updates sets the agenda by seating order, so the one item that needs the group lands wherever its owner happens to sit. His fix is to move updates out of the room and into a shared document, on the principle that updates are for reading and meetings are for deciding. The 30-minute agenda has four blocks: three minutes of silent reading, nine minutes of a 3-3-3 check-in (what is working, what is stuck, the one thing to do), fifteen minutes to decide two items, and three minutes to assign owners and dates. Each team member writes three lines before the meeting (done, next, need from the team), and the third line builds the agenda. He answers two common objections, that the meeting is the only time the team sees each other and that nobody will write the updates. A worked example of a fourteen-person operations team shows meetings falling from seventy-five minutes to about thirty and decisions rising from one a week to three or four.
points: A round of verbal updates scales badly: past six or seven people it consumes the hour and lets seating order decide which issue gets the group's attention.
Written three-line updates (done, next, need from the team) take about five minutes to write and three to read, and the third line sets the agenda.
The meeting is capped at two decision items of seven minutes each, so a decision is made or a named person is assigned to make it by a stated day.
Replacing 'let's take that offline' with a named owner and a deadline stops issues, like an expiring supplier contract, from disappearing.
The social value of the meeting survives in the 3-3-3 block, and a team that wants more time together should schedule it deliberately.
quotes: The fix is to move the updates out of the room. Updates are for reading. Meetings are for deciding.
Fourteen updates at three or four minutes each is fifty minutes of talking.
Most of each update matters to one or two people in the room.
And the round puts the one item that needs the group wherever its owner happens to sit in the running order.
Three minutes of everyone reading the same thing at the same time gives the room a shared starting point.
Two is the limit. A third item gets rushed, and you should save a rushed decision for next week.
The written updates hold the information. The 3-3-3 is where the team hears each other.
Write yours first, and write it well. The team copies the length and tone of the first update in the doc.
